plan: Complete enhanced-ACT literary narrative (CLD-P-ACT-R-000036, 'Shock Absorber'), about 600 words: a teenager who interprets for a parent realizes, at a sibling's parent-teacher conference, that years of softened translations kept the father from responding for himself. Story checked against every existing passage opening and against the WORKER.md list of covered narratives (no mentor/apprentice, closing shop or inheritance plot; no interpreter or parent-teacher passage in any verbal bank). 9 questions, 3 aimed at cross-paragraph inference. Relabelled to the blind solvers' rating where it was lower: R036-02 medium→easy, R036-03 medium→easy, R036-04 medium→easy, R036-06 hard→easy, R036-07 hard→medium, R036-08 medium→easy, R036-09 hard→medium.

passages.title: Shock Absorber
passages.text:
By the time I was twelve I had a second job that no one paid me for. At the bank, at the pharmacy, on the phone with the gas company, I stood beside my father and turned his sentences into English and the clerks' sentences back into the language we spoke at home. I was good at it. I was fast, I knew which words the clerks wanted to hear, and I had learned that a request delivered politely in English got further than the same request delivered the way my father said it, which was the way a man asks for something he believes he has already paid for.

So I adjusted. It seemed harmless. When my father told the man at the gas company that the bill was a theft, I told the man there seemed to be a mistake. When the pharmacist said, with a tight smile, that she had already explained the dosage twice, I told my father she was happy to explain it again. Everyone stayed calm. Things got done. I thought of myself less as a translator than as a kind of shock absorber, taking the jolts out of every conversation before they reached the other side.

The parent-teacher conference for my brother, Tomas, was in March. He was nine, bright, and in trouble for talking in class, and his teacher, Ms. Pruitt, had asked to meet with "Tomas's father and an interpreter." The interpreter was me. Tomas sat in the hall outside, swinging his feet.

Ms. Pruitt was kind and direct. Tomas interrupted, she said. He finished other children's sentences for them, and when he was corrected, he argued. "He's very smart," she added, "but he treats every conversation as if it belongs to him." I opened my mouth to translate and heard myself begin, "She says Tomas is very smart and talks a lot," and stopped.

It was not the sentence I had been given. It was the sentence I would have wanted to hear. And I realized, sitting in that small chair with my knees near my chin, that I did not know what my father would have done with the real one, because for years I had never let him have it.

My father was looking at me. So was Ms. Pruitt. I started again, and this time I gave him everything: the interrupting, the arguing, the conversations that belonged to Tomas. It came out slower than my usual translations, with pauses where I would normally have smoothed. My father listened without moving. When I finished, he was quiet for a long moment, and I braced for the sharpness I had spent years catching before it landed.

Instead he laughed, a short, surprised laugh, and said something I did not translate right away. Then I did. "He says Tomas gets it from him," I told Ms. Pruitt. "He says he will talk to him, and he says thank you for telling him straight."

On the walk home, Tomas ran ahead, kicking at slush. My father walked beside me and, after a block, said in our language that I had been quiet in there. I said I had been trying to get it right. He nodded as if that were obvious, as if it were what he had assumed I had been doing all along, and I did not have the heart, or maybe the nerve, to tell him otherwise.

candidates.stem: Which of the following best states a central idea of the passage?

choices.A: The narrator learns that the father is far more patient with teachers than with clerks.
choices.B: Years of softened translations had kept the narrator's father from responding for himself.
choices.C: The narrator discovers that Tomas's teacher has misjudged Tomas's behavior in class.
choices.D: The narrator decides that the family should stop relying on the narrator to translate.

candidates.evidence: for years I had never let him have it
candidates.explanation: The narrator's habit of smoothing every exchange meant the father never heard criticism as it was given. At the conference, an exact translation lets the father respond for himself, and he responds well.

A.rationale: The father's patience is not compared across settings; what changes is what he is told.

C.rationale: The father accepts the teacher's description and says Tomas 'gets it from him.'

D.rationale: Nothing suggests the narrator will stop translating.

hints: What had the narrator been doing for years, and what did it prevent?
candidates.remember: A central idea in a narrative often comes from a character's realization.

candidates.stem: In paragraph 2, the narrator's description of being "a kind of shock absorber" mainly suggests that the narrator:

choices.A: protected the father from people who were trying to cheat him.
choices.B: absorbed blame for mistakes that other people had made.
choices.C: stopped conversations before they could turn into arguments.
choices.D: softened each side's words so that neither felt their full force.

candidates.evidence: taking the jolts out of every conversation before they reached the other side
candidates.explanation: The two examples soften words in both directions (the father's 'theft' and the pharmacist's impatience), so the narrator took the force out of what each side said.

A.rationale: The narrator softened the father's words too, such as calling a 'theft' a 'mistake.'

B.rationale: The narrator never takes blame; the narrator changes what is said.

C.rationale: Conversations went on; the narrator changed their tone, not whether they happened.

hints: Whose words did the narrator change in paragraph 2?
candidates.remember: Test a metaphor against every example the passage gives.

candidates.stem: The narrator's statement that the father made requests "the way a man asks for something he believes he has already paid for" (paragraph 1) suggests that the father's manner was:

choices.A: blunt, as though he were already owed what he asked for.
choices.B: humble, as though he fully expected to be refused.
choices.C: confused, as though he did not quite know what he wanted.
choices.D: dishonest, as though he had not actually paid for it.

candidates.evidence: the way a man asks for something he believes he has already paid for
candidates.explanation: Asking for what you believe you have already paid for is demanding rather than polite, which explains why the narrator reworded his requests.

B.rationale: Someone asking for what he has paid for expects to receive it.

C.rationale: Nothing suggests confusion; the comparison is about entitlement.

D.rationale: The comparison describes his tone, not his honesty.

hints: How do people usually ask for something they have paid for?

strategy.explanation: Picture the tone of such a request.

candidates.remember: Comparisons describe manner as well as content.

candidates.stem: The narrator stops in the middle of the first attempt to translate Ms. Pruitt's remarks (paragraph 4) mainly because the narrator:

choices.A: cannot think of a word in the home language for "interrupt."
choices.B: sees that the father already understood the teacher's English.
choices.C: notices that the words soften what the teacher said.
choices.D: is worried that Tomas, waiting in the hall, can hear them.

candidates.evidence: It was not the sentence I had been given.
candidates.explanation: The narrator begins with 'very smart and talks a lot,' a softened version of 'treats every conversation as if it belongs to him,' and stops on recognizing the habit.

A.rationale: The narrator has the words; the problem is what the narrator chose to say.

B.rationale: Nothing suggests the father understood; he waits for the translation.

D.rationale: Tomas is outside, and the narrator never mentions being overheard.

hints: What is different between the teacher's words and the narrator's?
candidates.remember: Compare what a character says with what the character was told.

candidates.stem: In paragraph 3, the short sentence "The interpreter was me" mainly serves to:

choices.A: show that the formal role of interpreter fell, as usual, to the narrator.
choices.B: suggest that the narrator resented being asked to interpret again.
choices.C: reveal that the father had hoped to hire a professional interpreter.
choices.D: show that Ms. Pruitt had expected the narrator to come to the meeting.

candidates.explanation: Ms. Pruitt asked for 'an interpreter,' as if for a separate professional; the flat reply 'The interpreter was me' shows that the role went, as it always did (paragraph 1), to the narrator, the family's unpaid translator.

B.rationale: The narrator describes being 'good at it' and never expresses resentment.

C.rationale: Nothing says the father wanted a professional.

D.rationale: Her request for 'an interpreter' does not say she expected the narrator.

hints: What does the teacher's request assume about who will interpret?

strategy.explanation: Read the sentence before it and the details that follow.

candidates.remember: A very short sentence after a longer one often makes a pointed reply.

candidates.subskill: How an outcome bears on an expectation
candidates.stem: The father's response in paragraph 7 most directly shows that the narrator's long-held expectation about him was:

choices.A: correct, since he reacted sharply before he agreed with the teacher.
choices.B: irrelevant, since Tomas had already told him about the trouble in class.
choices.C: partly correct, since he thanked the teacher but refused to talk to Tomas.
choices.D: mistaken, since he took the teacher's criticism with good humor.

candidates.evidence: Instead he laughed, a short, surprised laugh
candidates.explanation: The narrator 'braced for the sharpness,' but the father laughed, admitted Tomas 'gets it from him,' and thanked the teacher for being direct, the opposite of what the narrator expected.

A.rationale: He was quiet, then laughed; he did not react sharply.

B.rationale: Nothing says Tomas had told him anything.

C.rationale: He says he will talk to Tomas.

hints: What did the narrator brace for, and what happened instead?

strategy.explanation: Compare paragraph 6's last sentence with paragraph 7.

candidates.remember: 'Instead' often marks the moment an expectation fails.

candidates.stem: When the father says that "Tomas gets it from him" (paragraph 7), he most likely means that:

choices.A: Tomas learned to interrupt by watching his older sibling translate.
choices.B: he recognizes his own manner of speaking in Tomas's behavior.
choices.C: he is responsible for Tomas's being so smart in class.
choices.D: he had expected Ms. Pruitt to blame his parenting.

candidates.evidence: He says Tomas gets it from him
candidates.explanation: The teacher describes a child who treats conversations as his own; paragraph 1 describes the father's own demanding way of speaking. The father sees himself in his son.

A.rationale: He says Tomas gets it from him, not from the narrator.

C.rationale: The remark responds to the description of Tomas's interrupting and arguing, not to his intelligence.

D.rationale: He takes responsibility on his own; nothing suggests he expected blame.

hints: What does paragraph 1 say about how the father speaks?
candidates.remember: A remark can make sense only when connected to an earlier description.

candidates.subskill: Meaning of a word in context
candidates.stem: As it is used in paragraph 7, the word "straight" most nearly means:
candidates.evidence: thank you for telling him straight
candidates.explanation: The father thanks the teacher for describing Tomas's behavior directly and honestly, as the narrator finally translated it.

A.rationale: The point is how directly she spoke, not how soon.

D.rationale: Nothing in the sentence concerns being alone.

hints: What had been missing from the narrator's earlier translations?

strategy.explanation: Predict a word that fits 'telling him ___.'

candidates.remember: Idioms like 'tell it straight' mean speak frankly.

candidates.stem: On the walk home, when the father says that the narrator "had been quiet in there" (last paragraph), he is most likely referring to the narrator's:

choices.A: slower, more careful translating during the meeting.
choices.B: refusal to answer Ms. Pruitt's questions about Tomas.
choices.C: decision to let Tomas wait outside in the hall.
choices.D: silence while the father laughed at Ms. Pruitt's remarks.

candidates.evidence: It came out slower than my usual translations, with pauses where I would normally have smoothed.
candidates.explanation: The narrator spoke throughout the meeting, so 'quiet' cannot mean silent. It fits paragraph 6: this time the translation 'came out slower,' with pauses, unlike the narrator's usual fast, smooth delivery.

B.rationale: The narrator answered nothing on Tomas's behalf; the narrator translated.

C.rationale: Tomas waited outside before the meeting; the father's remark is about the narrator in the meeting.

D.rationale: The father laughed and the narrator then translated his reply.

hints: Did the narrator actually stop talking in the meeting?

strategy.explanation: Find where the narrator's speaking changed.

candidates.remember: When a literal reading is impossible, look for the change the remark notices.

revision_log.reason: Round-2 solves matched every key; both flagged R036-05's key ('still young ... a role meant for an adult') as resting on an unstated age. Reworded the key to what the text supports (the formal role fell, as usual, to the narrator) and updated its explanation. Whole batch re-solved blind.

Round-1 blind solves (both matched every key, minor flags only) found that 01, 05, 06 and 09 all tested the same insight and that 01-B and 06-D partly cued 05 and 09. Replaced 05 (now the irony of 'The interpreter was me') and 09 (now what the father means by 'quiet'), and reworded 06's key. Passage unchanged. Whole batch re-solved blind.
